'''Ernst Homburg'''  (born 2 August 1952 in [[Venlo]]) is a Dutch emeritus professor of History of Science and Technology at [[Maastricht University]].<ref name=UMaastricht>{{cite web |url=https://www.maastrichtuniversity.nl/e.homburg |title=Dr Ernst Homburg |publisher=[[Maastricht University]] |access-date=2019-04-24 }}</ref> He published on the History of Chemistry and Technology in the 19th and 20th century in the Netherlands and Europe.

== Biography ==
Ernst Homburg was born in Venlo, the Netherlands, on 2 August 1952.{{sfn|Curriculum|2014}}
From 1964 to 1969 he was educated at the Protestant Lyceum (nowadays Huygens Lyceum), [[Eindhoven]]. From 1969 to 1978 Homburg studied chemistry at the [[Free University Amsterdam]] and at the [[University of Amsterdam]]. At the Free University he followed a course in the [[History of Science]] by Professor [[Reijer Hooykaas]], one of the Dutch pioneers in this field. Homburg wrote a thesis on the Disproportionation of Propene.

In 1978 and 1979 he worked at the Department of Pharmacy of the [[University of Groningen]] and from 1979 to 1983 he was research fellow in the History of Science in the Chemistry Department of the [[University of Nijmegen]]. Here he worked on a study of the development of the dye industry, supervised by Willem J. Hornix.{{sfn|Homburg|Belt|Hornix|1981}} From 1984 to 1993 he was assistant professor for 'Chemistry and Society' at the same department. In the period from 1989 to 1993 he was also a part-time assistant professor for History of Technology in the Department of Philosophy and Social Sciences of the [[Technical University Eindhoven]].<ref name=UMaastricht /> 

In 1993 he received his Doctorate in History at the University of Nijmegen with a dissertation entitled ''Van beroep "Chemiker": De opkomst van de industriële chemicus en het polytechnische onderwijs in Duitsland, 1790-1850'' ("Chemiker" by occupation : the rise of the industrial chemist and polytechnic education in Germany, 1790-1850).{{sfn|Homburg|1993}} His supervisor was dr. P.M.M. (Paul) Klep (Professor of Economic and Social History). 

From 1993 to 2001 Homburg became assistant professor History of Technology in the Department of History of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences of [[Maastricht University]]. This period was followed by a full professorate at the same institute on a chair endowed by the Dutch Stichting Historie der Techniek (SHT) (Foundation for the History of Technology).<ref name=Maastricht>{{cite web |url=https://www.maastrichtuniversity.nl/e.homburg |title=Dr Ernst Homburg |publisher=[[Maastricht University]] |access-date=2019-04-24 }} See also: {{cite web |url=https://www.histech.nl/www/en/about/bijzondere-leerstoel |title=Special chair: Ernst Homburg |publisher=Foundation for the History of Technology (nl) |access-date=2019-04-26 |archive-date=2019-04-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190425210850/https://www.histech.nl/www/en/about/bijzondere-leerstoel |url-status=dead }}.</ref>

In August 2018 he retired.

== Awards, honours and fellowships ==
In 1993 Ernst Homburg was senior research fellow at the Sidney M. Edelstein Center of the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]].<ref name=UMaastricht />

In 1998/1999 he was a fellow at the [[Netherlands Institute of Advanced Study]], [[Wassenaar]].<ref name=NIAS>{{cite web |url=https://nias.knaw.nl/fellow/homburg-e/ |title=Homburg, E. |publisher=NIAS |access-date=2019-04-26}}</ref>

In 2002 he was a fellow at the [[Max Planck Institute for the History of Science|Max-Planck-Institut für Wissenschaftsgeschichte]] in [[Berlin]].<ref name=UMaastricht />

In 2014 Homburg received the [[HIST Award for Outstanding Achievement in the History of Chemistry]], from the Division 'History of Chemistry' ("Hist") of the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS).<ref name=HistAward>{{cite web |url=http://acshist.scs.illinois.edu/awards/hist_award.php
|title=Hist Award for Outstanding Achievement in the History of Chemistry
|publisher=[[American Chemical Society]], Division of the History of Chemistry
|access-date=2019-04-24
}} (From 1956 to 2001 the award of the ACS was called the [[Dexter Award]] for Outstanding Achievement in the History of Chemistry. From 2002 to 2009 the award was called the Sidney M. Edelstein Award for Outstanding Achievement in the History of Chemistry; not to be confused with the Sidney Edelstein Prize of the [[Society for the History of Technology]] (SHOT) – a book prize.)</ref>

In his dissertation, Homburg described the important transformations during the first half of the nineteenth century in the character and the organization of the chemical industries in Europe. The leading positions in the management of the factories were then for the first time taken by industrial chemists. This process, together with the formation of an occupational group of high social prestige, was especially visible in Germany. There was an important relation with the development of polytechnic education. Homburg considers the transformation of polytechnic and university chemical education more as a cause than as a consequence of the emergence of the occupation of the chemist.{{sfnp|Homburg|1993|p=564}}

Many scholars, that wrote about the development of the chemist's occupation in the context of the development of university education, like [[Joseph Ben-David]],<ref name=bendavid>{{cite book |first=Joseph |last=Ben-David |title=The Scientist's Role in Society |url=https://archive.org/details/scientistsrolein00bend |url-access=registration |date=1971 |oclc=752540243 |location= Englewood Cliffs, N.J. |publisher=Prentice-Hall|isbn=9780137965571 }}</ref> [[Bernard Henry Gustin]],<ref name=Gustin>{{cite book | last=Gustin |first=Bernard Henry |title=The emergence of the German chemical profession, 1790-1867 |date=1975 |oclc=63380150 |location=Chicago |publisher=University of Chicago}}</ref> [[Erica Hickel]],<ref name=Hickel>See for instance {{cite journal |last=Hickel |first=Erica |title=Pharmacy in Munich |journal=Pharmacy in History |volume=14 |issue=3 |date=1972 |pages=118–119 |oclc=5547726098}}</ref> [[Ingunn Possehl]],<ref name=Possehl>{{cite journal |last=Possehl |first=Ingunn |title=Wirtschafts- und sozialgeschichtliche Aspekte des preußischen Apothekenwesens im 19. Jahrhundert: (Teil I:) die Apotheken als Arbeitskräftereservoir für naturwissenschaftliche Berufe |journal=Pharmazeutische Zeitung |date=1981 |volume=126}} and {{cite journal |last=Possehl |first=Ingunn |title=Wirtschafts- und sozialgeschichtliche Aspekte des preußischen Apothekenwesens im 19. Jahrhundert: Teil II: die Apotheken als Arbeitskräftereservoir für naturwissenschaftliche Berufe |journal=Pharmazeutische Zeitung |date=1981 |volume=126}}</ref> [[R. Steven Turner]]<ref name=Turner>See for example {{cite journal| last=Turner |first = R. Steven |title=Justus Liebig versus Prussian Chemistry: Reflections on Early Institute-Building in Germany |journal=Historical Studies in the Physical Sciences |volume= 13 |issue=1 |date=1982 |pages=129–162 |doi = 10.2307/27757508 |jstor=27757508}}</ref> and [[Ulrike Köster]],<ref name=Köster>{{cite book |last=Köster |first=Ulrike |title=Der Beruf des wissenschaftlich ausgebildeten Chemikers: Seine Entstehung u. Entwicklung während d. 19. Jh. im deutschsprachigen Raum |language=de |date=1984 | location=Rostock |publisher = Univ. diss. |oclc=720945769}}</ref> had created the impression that the emergence of the chemical occupation was the exclusive result of the work of [[Justus von Liebig]] (1803-1873). The broader social perspective was lacking. No reference was made to the interplay between events in this particular domain of work and knowledge and the development of the social division of labour as a whole. Homburg tries to fill this gap in the main body of his dissertation. Especially the short period between 1830 and 1850 marked a radical change in the organisation of education. Apart from the changes in the German educational system, a "veritable revolution of the laboratory" occurred.{{sfn|Homburg|1993|p=569}} Especially the emergence of [[analytical chemistry]] caused the development of new laboratories, with smaller [[Laboratory equipment|apparatuses]], and the possibility to give laboratory instruction a more prominent place in chemical education.

The last part of the dissertation summarizes the new functions in which the chemically trained found their occupation.
